meta.title: Choosing a database for a new service
meta.description: A decision tree for a team starting a new service: four questions about data shape, write volume and access patterns lead to a type of database.

summary.headline: Start with managed PostgreSQL unless a clear need rules it out.
points: Relational data with transactions belongs in a relational database; scale alone rarely changes that.
Key-only access suits a key-value store, or a cache if losing the data is acceptable.
Large analytical scans go to a columnar warehouse, never the service's own database.

data.title: Beyond one primary's writes?
data.subtitle: Over 20k writes/s or writes in many regions

data.title: Distributed SQL
data.subtitle: Multi-region, strongly consistent
data.description: Costs more and adds latency to every write. Book an architecture review before you commit.

data.title: Managed PostgreSQL
data.subtitle: The default for most services
data.description: Point-in-time recovery, read replicas and the team's existing runbooks. Start here.

data.title: Read and written by key only?
data.subtitle: No queries on other fields

data.title: Is it the system of record?
data.subtitle: Losing it would lose data

data.title: Key-value store
data.subtitle: Durable, predictable latency
data.description: Design the keys around your access patterns up front; adding a query later is expensive.

data.title: In-memory cache
data.subtitle: Sessions, rate limits, hot reads
data.description: Fast but volatile: the service must still work, more slowly, if the cache is empty.

data.title: Columnar warehouse
data.subtitle: Fed from the service by events
data.description: The service keeps its own operational store and publishes events into the warehouse.

data.title: Document store
data.subtitle: Nested records, flexible fields
data.description: Fits records read and written whole, such as product catalogues or form submissions.

steps.title: Overview
steps.description: Start at the top and answer each question. Green is the default, violet a specialist store, orange needs a design review. The analytics branch opens folded; the steps unfold it.

steps.title: Relational data
steps.description: Orders, accounts and invoices have relationships and need transactions, so the only question left is write volume.

steps.title: PostgreSQL almost always
steps.description: Few services outgrow one well-sized primary. Only sustained heavy writes or writes in several regions justify distributed SQL.

steps.title: Key-only access
steps.description: If every read and write uses one key, a key-value store fits; if the data can be rebuilt, a cache is enough.

steps.title: Scans or documents
steps.description: Reporting over months of history belongs in a warehouse; nested records read whole suit a document store.
